title: Prompt-to-audio is the wrong interface for game music. I built House Band so an LLM writes the score instead (MIT, playable examples)
author: lerugray
selftext:
I've come around to a simple view: prompt-to-audio is the wrong way to use AI for game music.



When a model generates finished audio, it is optimizing for a plausible surface. To my ear, that usually means the statistical middle of its training data: competent genre signals, no real arrangement decisions, and nothing you can open up, argue with, revise, or reproduce exactly. It sounds like "music" in the abstract, which is why so much of it feels tacky to me.



But LLMs are good at a different layer. They can read and write structured representations: notes, chords, rhythm, form, instrumentation, and code. That is where a composer or a band actually works. So I built House Band around that distinction.



House Band is open source (MIT code). An LLM is optional, and it only ever writes or edits a score. There is no prompt-to-audio path.



Listen first: [https://lerugray.github.io/house-band/](https://lerugray.github.io/house-band/)

Repo: [https://github.com/lerugray/house-band](https://github.com/lerugray/house-band)



A score is readable JSON: tracks, steps, notes, kit and patch choices, and a seed. A deterministic WebAudio renderer turns it into a WAV plus a custody manifest. It has 14 drum kits (7 synthesized, 7 sampled), 32 instrument patches, an FX suite, and a performance pass. You can bring your own WAV samples, map them into kits, and start from your own songs.



The examples I care about most are the co-writes. For Appendix N, my Renoise sketches stay intact as my layer; House Band develops them with bass, counterlines, new sections, and arrangement. The site has before-and-after pairs and lists what was mine and what it added. All ten tracks from my game Darkness on the Edge of Town are also there, each playable and linked to its underlying score JSON.



That division of labor is the point. I make the musical choices. The model can help manipulate a legible score. The renderer obeys it. Nothing is hidden inside a one-shot audio blob. If a bassline is wrong, you can point to the note and change it. If a section is boring, rewrite the section.



I'm interested in whether other devs feel the same split: AI as a score-writing collaborator versus AI as a black box that hands you finished audio. Feedback and criticism welcome, especially from people actually shipping game music.

comments.author: lucianw
comments.body:
That sounds fascinating.

I know nothing about music. The tracks on your "listen first" demo all sounded really MIDI-like, like I remember from the mid 1980s with soundblaster audio cards and the first years of electronic pianos. Is that inevitable? Do you have some that aren't so "MIDI-ish"?

replies.author: lerugray
replies.body: Thank you! The MIDI sound was intentional for the games I'm designing frankly as most have a vintage aesthetic - so that's probably most just my own samples and taste, but you can upload any samples you like (you can get tons of cheap ones from places like samples from mars) which have all professionally recorded pieces of gear an LLM can play with. Probably helps me a little bit that I was a musician in a past life (https://lerug.bandcamp.com/music)

comments.author: MelodramaticShape
comments.body: This sounds horrible. Just generate audio with suno and transcribe to midi.

replies.author: lerugray
replies.body: lol yeah everything I've heard from Suno sounds like the worst parts about music from the 2010s and sounds like absolute cringe but to each their own, music being completely subjective

replies.author: MelodramaticShape
replies.body: I mean it sounds better than a cat and a piano tumbling around in a clothes dryer or whatever you're trying to emulate here.

comments.author: demon-lord-sword
comments.body:
It's an interesting approach. I actually found quite the opposite with Claude in that the training data was highly insufficient for Midi specifically. Things like layering an ensemble, varying timing to avoid mechanical sound, Foley, mix/EQ, and general melody writing. I grabbed a bunch of resources, especially when something stood out.   
  
Curious to hear your thoughts on the result: [https://youtube.com/shorts/CdaYZaxjlzo?feature=share](https://youtube.com/shorts/CdaYZaxjlzo?feature=share) & [https://youtube.com/shorts/KyUouV6NazY?feature=share](https://youtube.com/shorts/KyUouV6NazY?feature=share)
